title: Open Day at the Hillside Animal Rescue Centre

turns.speaker: Sandra
turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hillside Animal Rescue Centre. My name's Sandra, and I'm the volunteer coordinator here. Before we set off on our tour, let me give you a quick idea of the layout of the site, so you can find your way around later. You should all have the plan from the welcome desk in your hands.

turns.speaker: Sandra
turns.text: So, we're standing at the main gate, at the bottom of the plan. If you came by car, you'll have seen the car park — that's outside the site, to the left of the gate, along Mill Lane. Just inside the gate, on the left, is reception, where you picked up your plans. Directly opposite reception — so just inside the gate, on your right — is the education room. That's where our school groups meet, and there'll be a short talk on pet care in there at eleven o'clock. From the gate, the main path runs straight up the middle of the site. Follow it right to the far end and you'll come to the small-animal barn. That's where we keep the rabbits and the guinea pigs, and it's usually the children's favourite.

turns.speaker: Sandra
turns.text: Now, the cattery. People expect it to be next to the barn, but in fact it's on the left-hand side of the site, about halfway along the fence. We moved the cats there last year, because it's the quietest corner we have. Up beyond the cattery, in the far left corner, you'll see the pond — do keep little ones away from the edge, please. On the right-hand side of the site you can't miss the big oak tree. The fenced paddock just next to it belongs to Bramble and Bracken, our two donkeys. You're very welcome to watch them, but please don't feed them. Behind the oak, right in the far right-hand corner, is the veterinary clinic. It's a working surgery, so I'm afraid it's closed to visitors today. And if you've brought sandwiches, the picnic area is in the middle of the site, on the left of the main path as you walk up. There are tables and benches on the grass there.

turns.speaker: Sandra
turns.text: Now, while I've got you all together, let me explain what happens if you fall in love with one of our residents today — which, I warn you, is very likely. The adoption process has a few steps, but none of them is complicated. The first step is simply to visit us and spend some time with the animals, which you're doing already. If you find an animal that seems right for you, the next step is to complete an application form. Most people do that online, on our website, but there are paper copies at reception if you prefer. Once we've read your application, one of our volunteers will arrange a home visit. Please don't be nervous about that — we're not inspecting your housework. We just need to see that your home is safe for the animal you've chosen.

turns.speaker: Sandra
turns.text: If everything's fine, you then pay the adoption fee, which is ninety-five pounds for dogs and cats. That may sound a lot, but it covers all the animal's vaccinations, and before any animal leaves us it's fitted with a microchip, so it can always be traced back to you if it ever gets lost. And finally, you take your new friend home. We stay in touch during the settling-in period — that lasts two weeks, and one of our team will phone you during that time to see how you're both getting on. Right — that's more than enough from me. Let's start the tour at the small-animal barn, so everyone follow me up the main path, and do shout if you have any questions as we go.

Sandra says the cattery is "on the left-hand side of the site, about halfway along the fence", not next to the barn as people expect.
Sandra places the clinic "behind the oak, right in the far right-hand corner" — the paddock by the oak itself belongs to the donkeys.
Sandra says the picnic area is "in the middle of the site, on the left of the main path as you walk up".

questions.evidence: Sandra says the next step is "to complete an application form", which most people do online.

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 2 — A volunteer arranges a ______ to check the animal will be safe.
questions.evidence: Sandra says "one of our volunteers will arrange a home visit" to check the home is safe for the animal.

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 3 — Pay the adoption fee of ______ (this includes all vaccinations).
questions.evidence: Sandra says the adoption fee "is ninety-five pounds for dogs and cats" and that it covers all the vaccinations.

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 4 — Before collection, the animal is fitted with a ______.
questions.evidence: Sandra says "before any animal leaves us it's fitted with a microchip, so it can always be traced back to you".

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 5 — The centre phones you during the settling-in period, which lasts ______.
questions.evidence: Sandra says the settling-in period "lasts two weeks", during which one of the team phones to see how things are going.
